title: Battling AI fatigue as a designer and developer: a practical guide
text:
Battling AI fatigue as a designer and developer: a practical guide

AI is great, but it doesn’t have to take over your life

A warning about using AI for everything

Not too long ago, I needed a new app for writing down my expenses so I could better keep track of my money, so I searched the iOS App Store.
I found many apps for expense reports, for budgeting and money management in general, but something felt strange. As a UI Designer and a Front-end Developer, I can spot patterns in the designs, and these apps weren’t human-made.

Most of the apps I found were AI-generated, vibe-coded apps, and I didn’t really want to use any of them, so I decided to make my own expenses app.
I fired up Claude Code in my terminal and started making a web app, this web app I opened in Safari on iOS, and from there I used the “Add to Home Screen” feature to use it like a native iOS app, more or less.

I’m no stranger to Claude Code, I vibe coded apps and websites before — both for work and personal use, but this time it felt different.
At work I use AI all day every day, I code websites with Claude Code, I also generate designs in Figma using the same AI, I often draft emails and make them sound more robust or more professional with an AI assistant, sometimes I even let the AI draft the email itself.

Some of the projects I do are generated in Figma using AI prompts, then they are coded from the generated designs in Figma into real websites, using AI as well, and at the end they are sent to the client with a professional-sounding AI-generated email message with the live website link, AI did all the actual work.

This AI-based workflow I’m describing isn’t rare these days.

This AI-based workflow I’m describing isn’t rare these days, lots of people use AI for everything and Front-end development is often cited as the industry most disrupted by AI usage.

Still, I think that was why it felt strange using AI to vibe-code my personal expenses web app in my free time, I was offloading my free time into an AI workflow as well.

I realized this was a sign of “AI fatigue” as it is now known in the industry, and I found a few ways to make it better so I decided to share them in this article.

Try to limit your usage of AI

Not every task should go through ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or your AI assistant of choice. Even if this task could be done quicker, there is a sense of accomplishment in doing things on your own. To start with, I would recommend that if you use AI heavily at work, try to avoid using it in your personal life.

If you plan a vacation, you can plan it yourself like you used to do a decade ago, by searching Google and asking friends for recommendations. Will you miss some attractions? Possibly. Will it matter in the long run? Probably not.

It’s worth it if it gets you out of the AI mindscape that leaves you a mere participant in your own life; if it’s only in your work life, it will feel much more manageable.

As Tyler Durden told us in “Fight Club” (1999), “You are not your job” (see image above), if your job requires you to use a certain technology — it doesn’t mean YOU need to use it, only your office persona needs to. Your free time is your own.

Do the fun parts yourself

I know this part might be controversial, but small and easy tasks you can do yourself in the same amount of time as the AI — you SHOULD do yourself. Not only that, you should also do the fun parts yourself, instead of asking AI to assist, even if it means it will take longer to complete, because the fun part is for you, the AI won’t have fun for you.

Finding out what you feel is the fun part is subjective and everyone will have fun with different parts, some coders like the math of it all, some like to build the UI, I like to hand code the CSS animations, so I’m not asking the AI to do THAT part for me. I will animate it myself.

Also, I don’t ask the AI to write for me. Ever. Not this article, no WhatsApp, no Slack messages, nothing. If I send something into the world, I wrote it myself.

For me writing is thinking and I don’t want to outsource it to a machine.

I might consult the AI about the writing process, I might ask it for information, or a summary, for its opinion on my writing, but the writing itself is my own, the thinking behind it is my own, and the final decision on what to change is also my own. For me, writing is thinking, and I don’t want to outsource it to a machine, at least not yet.

Don’t be 100x more productive

If you’re using AI in your workflow to be more productive, you’re probably already between 5x to 10x more productive than you used to be. Trying to maximize this and become 100x more productive will lead you to obsession and self burnout, please don’t do that to yourself.

invest in work quality, not quantity.

I know it’s very tempting, you tell yourself you can make an entire year’s work in a week, or even less but please realize that work is endless, you will never get everything done, work will always fill more of your time. Beware of productivity paradoxes.
A better way is to stay 10x more productive and just work happier, not harder, not longer, just make work more satisfying, invest in work quality, not quantity.

Invest in the work itself and not in the pipeline that made you get there because no pipeline will work 100% of the time and you’ll get crazier and crazier trying to perfect the pipeline using new models, new apps or new methods, instead of perfecting the work that you do with the help of your AI pipeline.

You are not staying behind

Tech people will always tell you that you HAVE to use any new technology, or else you’ll be left behind, you’ll become irrelevant in the near future.
Let me tell you right now — you’re NOT staying behind by NOT trying any new AI assistant, any new coding app or by not using the newest models.

Whenever something becomes essential for your job, you will learn it then. You don’t need to prepare yourself in advance by knowing all the digital tools in existence like you’re preparing for the digital apocalypse. Tools will come and go and they rarely matter in the great scheme of things.

You don’t need to prepare yourself in advance by knowing all the digital tools in existence like you’re preparing for the digital apocalypse.

Let me give you an example from my own job history, I remember when Sketch first came out, it was a UI Design software that was built from the ground up for UI Designers, any design software before it was a general purpose tool like Adobe’s Illustrator or Photoshop.

Many of my friends jumped on it, learning it early on and working with it as much as they could on their own jobs, trying to convince their managers to invest in a new design tool and blazing new workflows for it.

I didn’t do that, since Sketch was Mac-only and I was on Windows pre-2020 I waited, still using Adobe’s apps in the meantime. A couple of years later Figma came along (and won the UI Design software game).

I of course learned Figma but by not learning Sketch I was less tired of design tools compared to most of my peers, I managed to become a Figma expert much quicker and I didn’t need to convince my managers to abandon Adobe-based workflows as many already abandoned them for Sketch a year or two before.

Most of the times picking the winning technology, once it becomes clear, will be a much better strategy than learning all the new tools thinking you’ll otherwise be left behind. You’ll just tire yourself of technology all together.

Conclusion

Feeling fatigued about AI is natural, as it seems AI has completely taken over every aspect of our lives, but here in this article I outlined some key points that worked for me.

Leaving the AI at work feels liberating, it felt like in the early 2000s we left the internet at our home computers and never thought about it until we got back home.

Also letting go of some misconceptions I had about being 100x more productive, or about being left behind, which are ideas you hear all the time, either from your peers or from social media but aren’t in any way grounded in reality.

Ironically enough — my expenses app, froggo, that started all of this and made me write this article, is still an app I use every day to track my money and it earned its spot on my iPhone’s home screen.

Those are some of the tips that worked for me, but I saw many more tips online when I was doing research for this article, and I’m sure many people have their own strategies.

If you find something that worked for you and can also work for others, please leave it as a comment, I read all the comments and I can’t wait to see what worked for other humans.

And remember, AI usage can really affect your mood, so use it wisely.
Thanks for reading to the end 🙏

Further Reading

Beware of Productivity Paradoxes / Cal Newport

AI Fatigue is Real and Nobody Talks About It / Siddhant Khare

How I Broke Free from AI Fatigue / Kessie — Elevate Squad

How AI is quietly exhausting you — and what to do about it / Fast Company

What to do against AI Fatigue in your company? / Geoffroy de Lestrange

AI Fatigue Is Real — You’re Not Behind, Just Overstimulated / Tajinder Singh

Artificial Intelligence and Giving Up on Life / Robin VanGilder

title: The UX of contrast: lessons from Indika’s game design
text:
The UX of contrast: lessons from Indika’s game design

Introducing PX Contrast: a deliberate layering of conflicting player experiences leading to intentional multiple interpretations

Contrast is one of the most familiar visual tools for guiding attention in design. But in Indika it becomes a game UX tool. It shapes how players interpret the story. Released in 2024 by Odd Meter, the game won Best Narrative at the Games for Change Awards 2025 for its unconventional storytelling.

I first played Indika on release, and one thing kept bothering me: why do different parts of the experience look like they belong to completely different games? Its gameplay, sound, progression, and UI constantly pull against player expectations, yet together they express the same emotional conflict.

I call this approach Player Experience Contrast (PX Contrast): a sustained state where conflicting player experiences coexist, allowing players to hold different interpretations of the same interaction at once.

https://medium.com/media/2a925068042b626efe9447adfeba287f/href

A nun, a Devil, and a World that Stops Making Sense

You play as Indika, a young Orthodox nun who moves from complete obedience to rejecting her faith entirely. She carries the Devil with her, quite literally, inside her head, as she searches for identity outside the monastery walls. He whispers things Indika would never dare to say out loud, and raises questions she initially experiences as sinful. As the game progresses, the line between his voice and her own becomes increasingly blurred.

That internal split shows up in the world around her, too. At first, Indika feels surprisingly grounded. The game opens in a monastery that looks entirely believable. Growing up in Russia, I immediately recognized the monastery’s visual language, and that familiarity made the later transformation of the world feel even more unsettling.

As the game progresses, that realism breaks down the same way Indika’s certainty does. Historical accuracy gives way to dream logic: a cow the size of a barn, steam-powered machinery, ginormous bells, and many other bizarre things. The further you go, the less “real” the world becomes and the less sure Indika is of what she believes.

The world she discovers can only be described as a wild combination of comedy and tragedy straight out of the novels by Dostoyevski and Bulhakov.
— From the game’s official Steam page

That description captures the game’s tone remarkably well. It swings constantly between dark comedy and genuine dread, wrapping its story in symbolism and dream logic. Even the name “Indika” feels deliberate. Its resemblance to Cannabis indica adds another possible layer of meaning, especially given the game’s recurring themes of altered perception and reality.

That symbolism also reflects creator Dmitry Svetlov’s own experience. In an interview with The Guardian, he described growing up religious before becoming an atheist. Rather than criticizing faith itself, the game explores the broader system of beliefs and values that shapes a person’s identity.

Like any strong symbolic work, it invites multiple interpretations. What follows is my reading of the game and the role I believe its game UX design plays in supporting it.

Defining PX Contrast: Three Conditions for Meaningful Contradiction

PX Contrast builds on existing discussions of contrast in game UX (e.g., Salama’s Affinity vs Contrast framework), but extends the concept beyond momentary friction or immersion-breaking elements that pull players out of the experience.

PX Contrast is a deliberate layering of conflicting player experiences that coexist without resolution, allowing players to hold multiple interpretations of the same interaction simultaneously.

The term contrast here does not simply mean visual difference or opposing elements placed next to each other. In PX Contrast, the difference between systems creates a contradiction in how the player interprets the experience and feels the tension.

PX Contrast works when three conditions are met:

  1. Two or more systems (interface, sound, pacing, progression, environment, and others) create different interpretations of the same experience, allowing contrasting meanings to coexist.
  2. The contrast between these elements serves the same underlying theme, rather than existing as a purely aesthetic or mechanical choice.
  3. The contrast is intentional. It is a deliberate design choice that supports the player’s interpretation, rather than an unresolved inconsistency.

PX Contrast vs. Ludonarrative Dissonance

The other closely related term is ludonarrative dissonance, coined by Clint Hocking in 2007, describing moments when a game’s story and its mechanics pull in different directions. Since then, some designers and critics have started treating it as a deliberate tool rather than something to avoid. Connor Jackson, for instance, has argued for moving away from Hocking’s framing of the concept as a flaw, toward seeing it as a meaningful expressive device.

Dissonance describes the player’s feeling of mismatch, while PX Contrast describes the design structure that creates that tension. Not just gameplay versus narrative, but interface, sound, pacing, progression, and environment all contributing to the same emotional tension.

How Indika Uses PX Contrast

In Indika, the player and the protagonist share the same fractured perception: sacred rituals collide with gamified mechanics, slow reality with fast memories, and distorted spaces with normal ones. Neither side wins, creating a sustained tension that mirrors Indika’s inability to resolve her faith.

As a case study of PX Contrast, the game’s interface, pacing, and sound each pull against player expectations in different ways. Yet rather than creating noise, these сonflicting systems converge to teach players how to see the world through Indika’s broken perspective.

1. The Interface: Turning Faith Into Feedback

What also caught my attention was how the interface itself became part of the storytelling and how it shaped the way I experienced the main character’s journey. Rather than supporting the fiction of the world, it creates distance from it, aligning the player’s perspective with Indika’s own experience.

The interface gradually reshapes player expectations: actions that should feel sacred are reframed as ordinary gameplay interactions. That mirrors Indika’s own emotional detachment from her faith (she “plays” rather than truly believes). Religious rituals have stopped meaning anything. They’re just points in a mind game now. The interface teaches players to hold sacred and gamified readings at once without choosing.

This interpretation is also reflected in Svetlov’s own words:

The Game became a very important metaphor for our story. The game we all play, according to rules we didn’t make up, waiting for the reward that’s destined for us in case of “victory,” and living in fear of punishment in case of “defeat.”
— Dmitry Svetlov for Game Developer
https://medium.com/media/8b66af106072fe210230da9a71869fd8/href

One question the game raises from a design perspective is whether this spacial UI elements appearing near the character is deliberately non-diegetic (visible only to the player, not part of the game world), or whether Indika can actually perceive these game interface elements as part of her own mental reality.

I don’t think the game provides a definitive answer, and that’s what makes the question so interesting. Both interpretations contribute to PX Contrast, expanding the storytelling through intentional design.

  • If the UI exists only for the player, it creates distance between the player and the world.
  • If Indika can see it too, the interface becomes another expression of her fractured perception, extending the idea that the world we experience is shaped by her state of mind.

The game’s mechanics contradict the meaning these rituals appear to have within the world. Lighting candles and praying are not presented as moments of spiritual reflection, but as actions that generate points and rewards.

Normally, this gap between gameplay and narrative would be considered a design inconsistency. Here, the inconsistency becomes intentional feedback about the character’s internal conflict.

2. Sound: When a Prayer Sounds Like a Reward

Sound in Indika runs on the same contrast logic as the UI, and it’s easiest to see when you break it into a sequence:

  1. What the player does
  2. What they expect to hear
  3. What they actually hear
  4. What that mismatch makes them feel

Indika lights a candle and prays. The action carries the weight of a real religious ritual, so the player naturally expects silence, reverence, or something restrained. Instead, the game answers with a bright, cheerful retro chime. The kind of sound that says “you did it” in Duolingo, not “you were heard” in a church.

The brain reads it as a small reward, a completed task. That reading collides directly with the religious meaning of the action itself, and the player is left holding both interpretations at once. It’s the same dissonance Indika feels toward her own faith: the gesture is still performed, but the meaning behind it has quietly drained away.

Instead of reinforcing the atmosphere traditionally, the sound design creates intentional friction between action feedback and emotional context. Sacred and unsettling sounds exist alongside cheerful game-like effects and UI, forcing the player to question how these elements can belong to the same experience.

https://medium.com/media/aa38bef22ee08ced3d3020403523c590/href

3. Pacing: Slow Devotion vs. Fast Memory

In the “real” game world, movement is slow and heavy. One of the first tasks, carrying buckets of water, takes real time and effort, which reinforces just how monotonous monastic life is.

In the “real” game world, movement is slow and heavy. One of the first tasks, carrying buckets of water, takes real time and effort, which reinforces just how monotonous monastic life is. The platformer sections inside Indika’s memories are the opposite: fast, reactive, and sometimes genuinely tense. That tonal shift in pacing is another strand of the same contrast running through the whole game.

In the racing section, the contrast between the “real” world and Indika’s memories becomes even more explicit. Indika asks how to control the vehicle, and the answer comes through literal button instructions embedded in the dialogue between the characters (not through the usual on-screen control prompt). The game’s rules for the player become part of the rules governing Indika’s own memory, blurring the boundary between the player’s reality and hers.

https://medium.com/media/8616099f5a80911a2fb278f612fd77ca/href

As the Devil’s influence grows, his voice becomes more persistent and the boundary between realities begins to collapse. The screen floods with red, the music intensifies, and his voice merges with distorted sounds, overwhelming Indika’s own presence. Then a short prayer pulls her back into “normal” reality: the colors return, the Devil’s voice disappears, but a low, muffled sound remains underneath.

Switching between these states turns contrast into a gameplay system: players learn to interpret changes in visuals, sound, and control as signals of Indika’s mental state.

https://medium.com/media/abaae94df2e6b91bff2325e6e0c152f1/href

4. The illusion of Progression

Like the rest of Indika’s design, the progression system borrows the visual and sound design of retro games while quietly questioning the meaning behind it.

Mechanically, the player interacts with a familiar progression system: unlocking perks in a skill tree and collecting points. But all this progression exists only to generate more faith points. It becomes a reward loop without meaningful progression, exposing the emptiness behind the system. The accumulation of points feels as hollow as the rituals that produce them.

This idea reaches its peak at the end of the game: after everything Indika goes through, she finally receives an endless amount of points while trying to fulfill her wish. Yet the reward she spent the entire game chasing turns out to be completely meaningless.

https://medium.com/media/e402de0a5be3f22dbb76ca0af46ee044/href

Ironically, the faith points matter not because of what they unlock, but because of what they never do. Their mechanical emptiness mirrors the emotional emptiness Indika feels toward rituals she can no longer truly believe in.

And although technically it doesn’t change anything, all players continue to collect these points, including the developers. I think it can be viewed as a small social experiment.
— Dmitry Svetlov for Game Developer

5. Environment: From Order to Ruin

The contrast in Indika extends beyond individual mechanics into environmental storytelling. The game begins in a clean, organized monastery. Its architecture creates order and stability. By the end, this image is completely reversed: the player arrives in a broken and distorted landscape filled with ruined houses, dirty streets, and warped windows. The world itself reflects the uncertainty and conflict that have been growing throughout the game.

The environment becomes another feedback system: as the world grows more distorted, players learn to read the space itself as a signal of how far Indika’s grip on reality has slipped.

This change is reinforced through camera perspective. The final sequence shifts from third person to first person, placing the player inside an already distorted world. Combined with the warped camera angle this makes the experience feel more unsettling. The player is no longer just watching a broken world but experiencing it directly.

Core UX signal: this shift changes not just what the player sees, but how much control and orientation they feel they have.

By creating such a strong contrast between the beginning and the end, Indika leaves space for interpretation. The game does not give a simple answer about what is real, what is faith, or what is illusion. Instead, it places the player inside that uncertainty and lets them confront the same contradictions that define Indika’s journey.

Five Ways to Design with PX Contrast in Mind

Indika shows that effective game UX does not always require traditional consistency. Sometimes intentional inconsistency can create meaning. PX Contrast shows how contradictions between systems can become coherent when they reinforce the same emotional idea.

A few practical takeaways I’ll carry into my next project:

  • Start from the meaning, not the mismatch. Before introducing contrast between two systems, define what emotional or thematic idea it should express. Contrast that doesn’t serve a specific idea reads as inconsistency, not design.
  • Repeat the same idea across several systems. A single contradictory detail is easy to dismiss as a bug. PX Contrast works when multiple systems carry a version of the same idea through different means, so the pattern becomes unmistakably intentional. Consistency of intent is what separates PX Contrast from ludonarrative dissonance.
  • Let one system contradict another to hold two readings at once. For example, the visuals may suggest one meaning while sound or controls suggest another. Neither has to be “correct.” The player holds both interpretations at once and that unresolved tension is what PX Contrast is designed to create.

Why it still stays with me

None of this requires knowing what Svetlov actually intended. Games, like any art form, keep generating interpretations their creators never planned for. The strongest ones leave room for that. Indika did that for me. I played it in 2024, and it still stays with me because every part of its design serves the same emotional truth: it creates contrast without trying to resolve it.

After all, we so often look for simple answers in art and so often remain dissatisfied when we’re left alone with uncomfortable unanswered questions. But isn’t that the best thing that any experience can give us?
— Dmitry Svetlov for Game Developer

That’s what I’ll check next time. When design feels “off”, the question isn’t whether the contradiction should be resolved. It’s whether the tension creates meaning and whether contradictory experiences reveal something meaningful about the player, the character, or the world.

If you’ve spotted this same pattern somewhere else (a game, an app, a piece of software) that seemed “inconsistent” on purpose I’d genuinely like to hear about it.

All screenshots and gameplay footage are my own captures from my playthrough of Indika unless a different source is credited.
